newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour calls for blue, white collar pact.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour calls for blue, white collar pact.

text.p: Labour leader Tony Blair, rallying his troops for a general election polls tip him to win, will on Tuesday call for a partnership between business and unions to unleash Britain's potential.

In his keynote speech to the party's last annual conference before the election, due in the next seven months, Blair was set to bang home his message that Labour under his leadership has moved from the left to the centre of the political spectrum.
Without making spending commitments the ruling Conservatives could use against him in the campaign, Blair was also expected to promise to make education his priority, aides said.
"You're witnessing a conference that's preparing for government," Labour deputy leader John Prescott told the BBC. "The big idea is... to unlock the potential our people.

"That's why Tony will be talking about "education, education, education'... For that we need to work with trade unions and business together to make sure that in partnership we can unlock this tremendous potential."

But Prescott, echoing economics spokesman Gordon Brown in his speech on Monday, declined to go into details on tax or spending plans, saying only: "We have to live within the political realities of the present stage of public finances."

Brown, who tempered his speech with the long-term promise to lower the starting rate of income tax to 10-15 percent from 24 percent, has led Labour's drive to portray itself as a new party which has ditched its old tax-and-spend policies.
The make-over has upset Labour traditionalists. But Blair has maintained an iron grip on the party as he has dragged it to the political centre, attracting thousands of new recruits.

Aides said he would deliver another reminder in his speech that Labour will keep its distance from the unions, promising to govern as "the political arm of the British people" and not just the voice just of the labour movement.

Labour, out of power since 1979, heads the ruling Conservatives in polls by more than 20 points. Blair aims to cement that lead by convincing voters that he, more than Prime Minister John Major, is in touch with their aspirations.

Major, whose party has won four consecutive terms of office but is now dogged by voters' belief it is out of touch, suffered a new blow on Tuesday when a Conservative MP dropped a legal fight against newspaper sleaze charges.

Neil Hamilton, who quit as a junior trade minister in 1994 after the Guardian alleged he had accepted cash in return for asking questions in parliament, maintains his innocence but said he could no longer afford to continue his libel fight.

But his decision was described by the Guardian's editor Alan Rusbridger as "one of the most astonishing cave-ins in the history of the law of libel" and the newspaper immediately repeated its allegations with additional details.
The row is likely to rumble on through next week's Conservative conference which Major is banking on to lift his flagging support and rally anxious party workers.
Labour was also hoping to reopen the chronic splits in the Conservative party over Europe.

Blair is expected to pledge that a Labour government would set a deadline of mid-1998 for the completion of the European Union's single market, although he will keep open his options on whether or not to join a European single currency.
Labour foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook said Britain need not decide whether or not to sign up for European economic and monetary union until the end of next year -- well after the election.
